method_card.title: Weighted Mean and Geometric Mean
method_card.content:
Sometimes a simple arithmetic mean is not appropriate because not all values contribute equally to the result. In these cases you need a more specialised average.

The weighted mean assigns a ‘weight’ to each value to reflect its relative importance. The formula is: \(\bar{x}_w = \frac{\sum (w \cdot x)}{\sum w}\) where \(w\) is the weight assigned to value \(x\). This is similar to calculating a mean from a frequency table — frequencies are a type of weight. Weighted means are used in index numbers, grade calculations with different component weightings, and price indices.

The geometric mean is used when values represent multiplicative change, such as growth rates, ratios, or percentage increases over successive periods. For \(n\) values \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\), the geometric mean is: \(G = \sqrt[n]{x_1 \cdot x_2 \cdot \ldots \cdot x_n}\). On your calculator, use the \(n\)th root function or raise to the power \(\frac{1}{n}\).

When is the geometric mean more useful than the arithmetic mean? Whenever the data represent ratios or rates of change. If a population grows by a factor of 1.2 one year and 1.8 the next, the average growth factor is the geometric mean \(\sqrt{1.2 \times 1.8} \approx 1.47\) — not the arithmetic mean 1.5. Using the arithmetic mean would overestimate the true average growth.
steps: For a weighted mean: identify each value \(x\) and its corresponding weight \(w\)
Multiply each value by its weight: calculate \(w \cdot x\) for every pair
Sum all products \(\sum (w \cdot x)\) and sum all weights \(\sum w\)
For the geometric mean: multiply all \(n\) values together, then take the \(n\)th root using your calculator
State whether the arithmetic or geometric mean is more appropriate and explain why in context

exam_context.marks: 2–4 marks for a weighted mean calculation; 2–3 marks for a geometric mean; up to 2 marks for justifying which mean is appropriate
exam_context.frequency: Higher-tier topic; appears on approximately half of Higher papers, usually alongside index numbers or growth rates

worked_examples.question: A student scores 70% on coursework (weight 3) and 50% on an exam (weight 2). Calculate the weighted mean score.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Weighted mean \(= \frac{310}{5} = 62\%\). The coursework component carries more weight, pulling the mean closer to 70% than a simple average of 60% would suggest.

worked_examples.question: A company’s profit grew by a factor of 1.4 in Year 1 and by a factor of 2.1 in Year 2. Calculate the geometric mean growth factor over the two years. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

steps.label: Step 1 — Identify the values
steps.content: Two growth factors: \(x_1 = 1.4\) and \(x_2 = 2.1\). We need the geometric mean of 2 values.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Geometric mean growth factor \(\approx 1.72\) (3 s.f.). This means the company grew, on average, by a factor of 1.72 per year over the two-year period.

worked_examples.question: Three items have prices: Item A costs £20 with weight 5, Item B costs £35 with weight 2, Item C costs £10 with weight 8. Calculate the weighted mean price. A student claims the arithmetic mean (£21.67) is more appropriate. Explain why the weighted mean is better in this context.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Weighted mean \(\approx £16.67\). The weighted mean is more appropriate because Item C (the cheapest at £10) is purchased 8 times, while Item B (the most expensive at £35) is purchased only twice. The arithmetic mean treats all items as equally important, giving a misleading higher average. The weighted mean reflects actual purchasing patterns.

bronze.display: Calculate the weighted mean of the values 6 (weight 4) and 10 (weight 6).

misconceptions.message: \(\sum (wx) = 6 \times 4 + 10 \times 6 = 24 + 60 = 84\). \(\sum w = 10\). Weighted mean = 84 ÷ 10 = 8.4. Don't just average 6 and 10.

bronze.display: A student scores 80 on a test (weight 1) and 60 on an exam (weight 3). What is the weighted mean score?
Calculate the geometric mean of 4 and 9.

misconceptions.message: Geometric mean \(= \sqrt{4 \times 9} = \sqrt{36} = 6\). Don't use \(\frac{4+9}{2} = 6.5\) — that is the arithmetic mean.

bronze.display: A price index grows by a factor of 1.1 in Year 1 and 1.1 in Year 2. What is the geometric mean growth factor?

misconceptions.message: \(G = \sqrt{1.1 \times 1.1} = \sqrt{1.21} = 1.1\). When all values are equal, the geometric mean equals the arithmetic mean.

bronze.display: The weights assigned to three components of a mark are 2, 3 and 5. What is \(\sum w\)?

misconceptions.message: \(\sum w = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10\). Always sum all weights before dividing.

bronze.display: When is the geometric mean more appropriate than the arithmetic mean?
options: When data represent multiplicative growth rates or ratios
When the dataset contains an outlier
When the data are negatively skewed

misconceptions.message: The geometric mean is designed for data representing multiplicative change (growth factors, ratios). The arithmetic mean is for additive data.

bronze.display: Calculate the geometric mean of 2, 8, and 8. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: \(G = \sqrt[3]{2 \times 8 \times 8} = \sqrt[3]{128} \approx 5.04\). Use the cube root (or raise to the power 1/3) on your calculator.

bronze.display: A weighted mean calculation gives \(\sum (wx) = 240\) and \(\sum w = 12\). What is the weighted mean?

silver.display: Three subjects have marks: Maths 72 (weight 4), English 65 (weight 3), Science 80 (weight 3). Calculate the weighted mean mark.
A company’s revenue grew by factors of 1.5, 1.2, and 1.8 over three consecutive years. Calculate the geometric mean growth factor to 3 significant figures.

misconceptions.message: \(G = \sqrt[3]{1.5 \times 1.2 \times 1.8} = \sqrt[3]{3.24} \approx 1.479\). Raise to the power 1/3 on your calculator. Don't use the arithmetic mean (1.5).

silver.display: A survey asks three groups their average weekly spending: Group A (40 people): £30, Group B (30 people): £50, Group C (30 people): £20. Calculate the weighted mean spending across all three groups.

misconceptions.message: Weights are group sizes. \(\sum (wx) = 30\times40 + 50\times30 + 20\times30 = 1200+1500+600 = 3300\). \(\sum w = 100\). Weighted mean = £33.

silver.display: An investment grows by a factor of 3 in Year 1 and shrinks by a factor of 0.75 in Year 2. Calculate the geometric mean growth factor to 3 significant figures.

misconceptions.message: \(G = \sqrt{3 \times 0.75} = \sqrt{2.25} = 1.5\). Include the shrinkage factor (0.75) as the multiplicative value — do not use negative numbers.

silver.display: A student says the arithmetic mean of growth factors 1.0 and 4.0 is 2.5, while the geometric mean is 2.0. Which correctly represents the average growth over two periods?
options: Arithmetic mean (2.5), because it averages the values directly
Geometric mean (2.0), because growth is multiplicative
Both are equally valid for growth data
Neither — you should add the growth factors instead

misconceptions.message: Growth is multiplicative: if you apply a factor of 1.0 then 4.0, the result is 4 × the original. The true average factor that gives the same result over 2 steps is \(\sqrt{1.0 \times 4.0} = 2.0\). Applying 2.0 twice gives \(2.0 \times 2.0 = 4.0\) — correct. Applying 2.5 twice gives 6.25 — wrong.

silver.display: A weighted mean is calculated with values 10 (weight 2), 20 (weight k), and 30 (weight 3). The weighted mean is 21. Find k.

gold.display: An index number series shows prices: Year 0 = 100 (base), Year 1 = 110, Year 2 = 121, Year 3 = 133.1. Calculate the geometric mean annual growth factor from Year 0 to Year 3. Give your answer to 4 significant figures.

misconceptions.message: The growth factors year-to-year are 110/100=1.1, 121/110=1.1, 133.1/121=1.1. Geometric mean \(= \sqrt[3]{1.1 \times 1.1 \times 1.1} = 1.1\). Alternatively, overall factor = 133.1/100 = 1.331. \(\sqrt[3]{1.331} = 1.1\).

gold.display: A school calculates a student’s grade from four components: Component P (weight 5), Component Q (weight 3), Component R (weight 2). Scores are P=74, Q=62, R=88. The student argues the simple mean (74.67) is fairer. Which statement is correct?
options: The simple mean is fairer because it treats all components equally
The weighted mean (74.1) is more appropriate because it reflects each component's relative importance in the overall grade
The weighted mean is only appropriate when weights are equal
The mode of the three scores should be used instead

misconceptions.message: Weighted mean = (74×5 + 62×3 + 88×2) / 10 = (370+186+176)/10 = 732/10 = 73.2. Component P carries the most weight by design, reflecting its greater contribution to the overall assessment.

gold.display: Population growth factors for a town over 4 years are: 1.03, 1.05, 0.98, 1.06. Calculate the geometric mean growth factor to 4 significant figures.

misconceptions.message: \(G = \sqrt[4]{1.03 \times 1.05 \times 0.98 \times 1.06} = \sqrt[4]{1.1237...} \approx 1.030\). Raise to the power 0.25 on your calculator.

gold.display: A house price index has weighted mean 125 across three regions. Region A (weight 3) has index 110, Region B (weight 5) has index 130. Region C has weight 2. What is the index value for Region C?

misconceptions.message: \(\sum w = 3+5+2 = 10\). \(\sum (wx) = 125 \times 10 = 1250\). Known contributions: \(110 \times 3 + 130 \times 5 = 330 + 650 = 980\). Region C contribution: \(1250 - 980 = 270\). Index C = 270 ÷ 2 = 135.

gold.display: Two datasets each have 4 values. Dataset A: 1, 2, 8, 32. Dataset B: 4, 4, 4, 4. Calculate the geometric mean of Dataset A and explain why it equals the geometric mean of Dataset B.

misconceptions.message: Dataset A: \(1 \times 2 \times 8 \times 32 = 512\). \(\sqrt[4]{512} \approx 4.76\). Dataset B: \(4^4 = 256\). \(\sqrt[4]{256} = 4\). The two geometric means differ because the products differ. The geometric mean measures the single value that, when repeated n times, gives the same product as the original data.
